July 2011 # Looking to China - Copper prices traded in a tight range during June due to investor sentiment for commodities remaining cautious and negative macroeconomic signals. However, when the Greek austerity package was approved and the euro recovered, the 3- month LME price rose to over $9,350/t on 30th June. This is the highest price since the end of April and is above the upper bounds of the recent trading range. - The Chinese market has been in deficit and, as their reliance on stocks to meet demand is coming to an end, their import demand should recover despite the notso-favourable SHFE/LME arbitrage and local credit tightness. - The European market is not as strong as expected earlier this year, while the US has stayed quiet. # Bound to change June saw the copper price trade in a tight $300/t range of $8,9009,200/t until the 29th . There was a similar story across the LME **Price ($/t) SHFE (RHS) LME (RHS) 11000** complex, as lead, zinc and aluminium also traded in tight ranges. Tin **Comex (RHS) LME Cash Price (LHS)** and nickel were the exceptions, having risen more than other metals, **10000 SHFE Cash Price* (LHS)** so continued to give back some of these gains in June. Copper price **9000** movements have been driven by short term swings in sentiment about **8000** the macroeconomic outlook due to the latest data releases. There has been little copper specific news to affect prices. The rise in **7000** uncertainty is weighing on investor sentiment, especially: how the **6000** Greek debt crisis will resolve itself; when the US will extend its debt **5000** ceiling; and how aggressive will central banks become in addressing inflationary pressures. This is reflected in the fact that open interest on **4000** the LME has continued to decline since its peak in January, indicating **3000 Jan-10 Apr-10 Jul-10 Oct-10 Jan-11** the liquidation of long positions along with some short covering. Data: LME, SHFE, Comex * SHFE price less 17% VAT converted into $/t Similarly, the CFTC data on Comex long and short positions shows a decline in both throughout 2011, with the net position having fallen from long in the period October 2010 to April 2011to almost neutral in June. However, investor sentiment has not gone bearish on copper, as there are no indications of a rise in short positions on either exchange. The volatility in sentiment meant that, as soon as the Greek Parliament approved the austerity plan on 29th June, the bounce in the value of the euro pushed all LME metals higher. 3-month copper closed at a two month high of US$9,320/t and was above $9,350/t as we went to print. ## **Most spot business in Asia...** Following a global deficit of over 100,000t in Q1, we estimate that the deficit almost doubled in the current quarter. China explains most of the shortage, as the world ex-China was practically balanced in H1. Those Chinese semi-fabricators who have not done so already have been consuming cathode from their stocks and all of those that can use scrap have increased their buying, as scrap availability has benefitted from continued high cathode prices. Expectations by some players in the market of Chinese restocking in Q2 have vanished, as consumers appeared to be foregoing any stock building as usually happens ahead of the summer holidays. This paves the way for mixed expectations in the market for Q3, which is typically the quietest tim

e of the year. Nevertheless, there is evidence of tightness of material in China. Tax-paid stocks in SHFE warehouses declined to 51,939t by the end of May – the lowest level since July 2009 - and increased slightly to fluctuate around 57,700t in June, while bonded SHFE material through 24th June declined to 23,010t, down by over 10,000t from their high in mid-May. Moreover, cathode stocks at bonded warehouses in China have also been dropping since April and, as our analyst in Beijing estimates, current levels are approaching the 200,000300,000t range which is considered to be a normal level for traders working stocks. We therefore see only modest inventory decline from now on. We see these reductions in stocks in China as a result of the deficit in the country in Q2. Continued strong growth in Chinese refined production has been more than offset by lower imports. In addition, consumers may not have been taking material to build up stocks but did need to buy more cathode to meet higher seasonal demand in Q2. This apparent need for material has also been putting pressure on scrap buying, the availability of which from domestic generation has benefitted from sustained high copper prices. Scrap discounts in June are much lower than in December, reflecting the tightening of the market. Given the extended period of a negative arbitrage and the run down in bonded stocks, consumers and traders may not be as covered for material as in previous months. If this is the case, they will need to be more active in © 2011 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 16 Copper Monitor July 2011 www.crumonitor.com the cathode market, which seems to be already happening. In the last two weeks of June we are aware of two private tenders for LME Grade A cathode from South American miners which settled with premiums around US$90-110/t cif Shanghai for material to be shipped in H2. In addition, a revival in buying interest can be seen in the fact that premiums for imported metal rose to $120-150/t cif China by the end of June, up from $100-135/t the previous week. As for non-LME registered Grade A cathode, the latest tender in Chile was awarded at $60 – see the table on page 5. Another sign that Chinese buyers are becoming short of material is that since mid-June the SHFE/LME arbitrage has been narrowing and opening intermittently. As a consequence of the arbitrage being firmly closed before this and administrative changes that some believe have led to a decline in the use of copper as a financing tool, an absence of international purchases saw Chinese cathode imports drop to 149,235t in May, the lowest level since November 2008. indications that Chinese market participants are considerably restricted by the tightness of credit and this is limiting their cathode purchases. Elsewhere in Asia, copper consumption is also strong, particularly as Japan recovers. For instance, wire & cable shipments by producers in Japan increased in May by 3% y-on-y. While still well below previous highs, this growth is a sign that the supply chain is recovering quite quickly from the earthquake and tsunami, and further down the line copper consumption is likely to recover more quickly than we previously thought. ## **... while Europe looks good, but not as good as the market was expecting** As for the demand situation in Europe, semi-fabricators appear to have enough supplies of metal from their annual contracts, given that they locked in more material than in 2010 ahead of expectations for a particularly tight 2011. Demand for semis products is reported to be good, but not as strong as producers were anticipating at the beginning of the year. As a result, there have been very limited needs for spot cathode in Q2 to build up additional inventory of semis to tide them over during the holiday shutdowns. Also, Europeans have been facing financial difficulties due to high copper prices and tough credit conditions, which have left them holding minimum levels of inventory and working on a hand-to-mouth basis. Premiums in Europe have remained in the US$80-100/t range Rotterdam seen last month, which is well above the low levels in March but generally below the benchmark annual contract level of $98/t. In addition, there continues to be good availability of scrap, which further eases the need for cathode from the spot market. In fact, we have heard that some semifabricators have again been taking scrap and selling back surplus cathode into the market. In the USA there is a similar scenario to that in Europe, as cathode consumers have been showing a steady need for material, which is being largely supplied via their annual contracts. Not surprisingly, spot business continues to be subdued and premiums have been remained in the 5.0-6.0¢/lb range. However, there are some pressures due to the seasonally high inland freight rates because of higher agricultural demand for trucks during the harvest season. Nevertheless, there have been large cancellations of warrants on LME material in the USA, which CRU does not believe is a sign of a demand recovery. Instead, we think that they may be related to warrant holders moving material out of LME warehouses given the lengthening times for material to be delivered out. This is the case for most metals but mainly aluminium, with delivery from the Detroit warehouse stretched out to over one year from now. Also, warehous

es may be competing on storage rents to attract more customers. These delays may also be helping to support copper premiums. Elsewhere in the US,

there appears to be good availability of high grade scrap, as collection is encouraged by high prices, while semis production growth and Chinese scrap buying continues to be subdued. 

## **A few disruptions in supply make some noise but have limited impact** 

On the supply side, in Chile some miners reported that a few cathode customers had asked for shipments delays, mainly to Europe. This, plus no significant disruptions to mine output, appeared to have created the opportunity for miners to tender some cathode as reported above. Among the few disruptions, operations in the region of Antofagasta, from where 75% of the exports of Chilean copper cathode came in 2010, suffered from unusual rains, an earthquake and some power cuts in June. Miners said that annual production will not affected, although some inconvenience is happening in the short run. North of Antofagasta, workers at the Iquique Port ended a 1-month strike in mid-June. Last year, just 7% of the Chilean cathode was shipped from this port with China as the main destination. Miners were able to ship from alternative ports, although at higher costs. At the time this strike ended, Collahuasi’s Patache Port was resuming operations after a 6-month stoppage due to an accident at their ship loader affecting their logistics for concentrate. In central Chile, contractor workers at El Teniente protested during most of June and operations had to run at reduced capacity. 

In Japan, the Onahama smelter is expected to re-start operations in July after being closed for around 4 months following the tragedy in March. We heard that there were some difficulties regarding port facilities, although it appears that the company has cleared up those issues. 

In Asia, power shortages scheduled for the summer are likely to affect copper smelters and could hit semis producers in China. The outcome is as yet unclear, but we expect it to limit refined production as well as scrap generation. Chinese buyers have already increased purchases of scrap No2 in the US over the past month, though volumes are not yet very large.  The Chinese have been absent from the European market for some months now and remain so. We heard that freight rates from Europe to China are very expensive and this may be discouraging such trade. There are indications that there has been considerable de-stocking of scrap in China and the lack of material has already been restricting refined production growth from secondary sources. 

## **A dull summer start clouded by uncertainty** 

We perceive an overall environment surrounded by uncertainty and mixed signals in China and Europe, while the US waits for a strengthening of recovery. China is always the key factor.  Last year in China,

Q3 did not have the usual slowdown in growth, and this year market participants cannot yet assess whether Chinese buyers will restrain their purchases or come back aggressively given the cathode deficit in the country. In Europe, the risk factors clouding the short term outlook are due to the macroeconomic environment, geopolitical uncertainty and volatility of the copper price. There is hesitation to invest in commodities at the moment despite the strong fundamentals and we have seen a general slowdown of fund activity since April. This sentiment is fed by uncertainty over the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis, the impact that this will have on the value of the US dollar, and a slowing in the pace of global economic recovery. The 3-month LME copper price traded in a US$8,897-9,195/t range for most of June. In order to break to the upside, the price needed to clear $9,265/t, which it did on the 29th . The next target is the short-term downward trend line from the recent highs at US$9,535/t. On the downside should the price break below $8,865/t then it could find support at US$8,750/t, with US$8,550/t the next level. We are sceptical of the sustainability of the Greek austerity plan, which at best gives banks more time to prepare for an eventual default and restructuring. Therefore, we expect the copper price to remain volatile in the next month or two, as macroeconomic developments and investor sentiment continue to dictate price movements. # Consumption trends 

## **Japanese autos severely impacted while rest of the industry grows** 

Interconnector assembly, which primarily serves the automotive, appliance and electronics industries, is a key consumption area for both copper and copper alloy plate, sheet, strip and foil.  Following the 11<sup>th</sup> March earthquake in Japan there was concern regarding which parts of the automotive supply chain would be affected, either directly or indirectly.  The **Japanese Automobile Manufacturers Association** reported that production by Japanese manufacturers in March and April was down by 52.3% and 60.1% y-o-y.  This was attributable to the effects of the disaster as some automotive production and component facilities were closed due to damage, power outages or evacuation.  In spite of the downside risk to supply chains, most automobile manufacturers and regions have managed reasonable growth including the US, Germany and China which were up by 6.8%, 19.1% and 18.5% y-o-y by volume in Q1 2011 respectively. 

## **Interconnect segment performs well in Q1 despite worries about recent monetary tightening in China and the disaster in Japan** 

The after-effects of the Japanese disaster upon major interconnector companies also appear to be minimal. Revenues for **Amphenol** , whose business comprises 93% interconnectors by sales, reported a rise in automotive-related revenues, up by 26% y-o-y in Q1 2011 which accounts for 8% of total sales.  Likewise, **Molex** posted strong Q1 auto component sales results and its exposure to the disaster was limited by its interest in diversified markets.  Demand from the information technology sector has driven growth for both companies due to increasing consumption of smart devices and particularly tablet computers with this sales area now making up 18% and 24% of total company revenue for Amphenol and Molex respectively. Meanwhile, China ratcheted up its monetary policy in attempts to stem inflation. This has resulted in a slowdown in Chinese industrial production within the electrical engineering sector.  This rose by 13.1% y-oy in Q1 2011 which is a good performance when considering the strength of the Q1 2010 results. Consequently, as the electrical and electronic products sector accounts for around 55% and 65% of end-use (2009 levels) of copper PSSF

and copper alloy PSSF there was an 8.9% y-o-y contraction in copper and copper alloy rolled products consumption levels for Q1 2011. 

## **Copper plate, sheet, strip and foil (PSSF)** 

World copper PSSF production rose to 482,000t, up by 1.5% y-o-y and sequentially in Q1 2011.  This represents a lower figure than we had previously estimated in April’s edition of copper flat rolled product consumption trends.  This is attributed to a deceleration in growth that was seen in the flourishing electrical engineering sector last year, which could not be sustained due to the negative impact of China’s tighter monetary environment.  At a national level there were notable changes seen in Germany which increased production by 7,000t to reach 52,000t, up by 15.6% y-o-y in Q1 2011.  This was attributed to strong domestic demand from the construction and automotive manufacturing industries, as well as the general consumer products sector which accounts for around 25% of global copper PSSF demand.  This has been recovering well after a poor 2009 and H2 2010. 

The **China Nonferrous Metals Association** reported that semis output dropped by 2.1% y-o-y in the first two months of 2011 and subsequently rose by 1.73% y-o-y in March and April 2011.  Such a pattern is likely the result of cyclical stocking behaviour of consumers influenced by volatility in the copper price. Overall, this is a positive sign for the Chinese copper flat rolled product market because semis production levels were very buoyant last year, rising 17.5% y-o-y on the back of a strong and full recovery in the Chinese electrical, electronic and general consumer product and construction markets.  While the Chinese market is unlikely to support equivalent growth rates this year, the construction sector of the developed

world is beginning to register signs of recovery after a long period of depression since the economic crisis. Copper PSSF is well positioned to benefit from an upturn in construction, as around 10% of its usage lies in this area, with it finding greater application in the type of high-end architecture traditionally more associated with Western building design. 

## **Copper alloy plate, sheet, strip and foil (PSSF)** 

The copper alloy PSSF business is strongly correlated with the copper PSSF product sector due to common end-uses, especially the interconnect segment.  Developments in the electrical and electronic, and consumer and general product markets, dictate demand for both copper and copper alloy PSSF. 

World production of copper alloy PSSF fell by 26,000t to reach 471,000t, down by 5.3% y-o-y in Q1 2011. As with Copper PSSF, actual first quarter data showed that global production and consumption of copper alloy PSSF were both lower than we had anticipated due to a recent slowdown in the electronic engineering sector after it enjoyed a booming 2010 in key regi

ons.  A larger proportion of total copper alloy PSSF enduse is by the electrical and electronic products sector than in the copper PSSF segment.  Given the greater level of dependency of copper alloy PSSF upon the electrical and electronic products sector it is unsurprising that alloy PSSF reflected the decelerating trend to a larger extent. 

The regional breakdown indicates that production in China was 168,000t in Q1 2011, whereas consumption was 204,000t in the same period.  This marks the second quarterly contraction in a row after three sequential quarterly rises from the beginning of 2010.  Chinese copper alloy PSSF output dropped by 18.7% and consumption shrunk by 22.0% sequentially in Q1 2011, as the market was impacted by soaring copper prices and a tightened credit environment resulting in end-use sectors undergoing destocking.  However, this trend conflicts with end use indicator data released by the **National Bureau of Statistics of China** .  The Bureau reports that domestic integrated circuit output has been increasing sequentially every quarter from Q1 2010 to Q1 2011 and has also risen in April and May.  In addition, it estimates that automotive production experienced a strong Q1 2011, rising by 3.6% sequentially and 10.0% y-o-y.  However, moving beyond this time period, automotive production dropped by 2% y-o-y in both April and May, perhaps signalling that the decline in copper alloy PSSF apparent consumption is only just beginning to show in indicators that monitor output from downstream product segments due to the aforementioned consumer destocking.  The increasingly difficult domestic trading environment in China during first quarter 2011 is also in evidence from the 2% shift in the share of global consumption from China to North America, which was more resilient on the back of the emergence of positive domestic economic indicators. 

North East Asian copper alloy PSSF production decreased by 12.8% y-o-y to 84,000t in Q1 2011, primarily attributed to the comparison with a strong quarter in 2010 which was in turn due to the positive impact of government subsidies in the wake of the economic crisis. Japan, the biggest exporter of copper alloy PSSF in the Asia region, was more resilient than initially expected in the face of cascading disasters throughout March.  Production in Japan amounted to 38,000t in Q1 2011, down by 15.6% y-o-y.  In addition, copper alloy PSSF output from both South Korea and Taiwan declined by 10.3% and 8.3% y-o-y in Q1 2011. Taiwan and Japan produce more copper PSSF than copper alloy PSSF, which is principally attributed to greater import demand from China, which is less self-sufficient in this product segment than copper alloy PSSF.  Data released by the **Japan Copper and Brass Association** suggests that domestic production of copper alloy sheet and strip declined by 13.5% y-o-y in April, while that of copper alloy sheet and strip shrunk by 1.5% y-o-y in the same month. # Industry News ## **Consumption** - Data released by the **Japan Copper and Brass Association** showed that Japan’s copper semis output rose to 72,328t in May 2011, a 2.4% m-o-m and 0.1% y-o-y increase. Production was supported by strong demand from energy efficient air conditioner makers, who raised production ahead of the peak demand season. This compensated for weak demand from the semiconductor and automotive sectors. - According to the **Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association** , copper wire and cable shipments totalled 51,200t in May 2011, up by 3.0% y-o-y, the first y-o-y increase in three months. Nonetheless, May shipments experienced an 8.9% m-o-m fall and remained the third lowest for May in 35 years. Japanese exports of copper wire and cable have been affected by China’s economic slowdown and domestic demand has been impacted by the decline in the automotive industry. - According to **Aurubis** , Chinese copper imports may increase in H2 2011, after the decline seen in H1. May imports contracted to 149,235t in May 2011 from 160,236t in the previous month. The figure was also down by 46.7% from the same period a year ago. Aurubis commented that Chinese copper demand was met by stocks in warehouses, which have been heavily down due to recent consumption. The European copper producer said that the fact that Chinese IP in May was strong may be an indication of strong underlying copper demand. © 2011 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 13 of 16 Copper Monitor July 2011 www.crumonitor.com - **Delphi Automotive** , a wiring harness maker, is opening a new manufacturing facility at Moldova Noua, Romania. The site will enable the company to produce wiring harnesses to meet increasing demand from automotive manufacturers across Europe. It will work closely with existing Romanian Delphi facilities. The project is being deployed over two phases; the company initially opened the Moldova Noua facility for testing in April and intends to open an additional 2,400 square metres in September 2011. - Chinese **Zhengwei International Group Co. Ltd.** will undertake a 250,000t/y copper wirerod project in Wuwei County of Anhui Province. **Anhui Xinke New Materials Co. Ltd.** , another Chinese fabricator, has also announced plans for a 120,000t/y copper wirerod project, which will take two years to develop at a cost of RMB665.6M. In addition, it was reported that **Nanya Copper Foil Co. Ltd.** intends to expand its electrolytic copper foil capacity from 34,000t/y to 45,900t/y with the construction of a new plant located in Kunshan, Jiangsu Province, due to start operations in September 2011. - **Mueller Industries Inc.** , a leading copper alloy rod, bar and section and copper tube producer in the US, expressed interest in expanding their producti

on facilities as well as diversifying their product range.  Mueller has placed a preliminary non-binding bid letter for the 100% purchase of unnamed copper producing assets based in Reading, Pennsylvania, owned by **Industrias Unidas SA de CV** and its subsidiary, United Copper Industries Inc. (UCI).  Mueller has allocated US$35-50M in cash for the purchase. The company has also expressed interest in buying an electrical building wire manufacturing facility in Denton, Texas. 

- **Furukawa Electric Co.** of Japan plans to begin exporting copper power cable from its Shenyang production plant in China to the US and Europe from September 2011.  So far, the company has been providing cables for the Chinese market only.  It was reported that the quality of cables has improved sufficiently to be exported to industrialised countries.  The company hopes to achieve annual sales of US$125M to industrialised countries in the next five years.  Furukawa Electric expects strong demand from sustainable sources of energy. 

- **Chinalco Luoyang Copper Co. Ltd.** , a Chinese high-precision copper plate and strip fabricator, plans to raise production by 18% y-o-y to 160,000-170,000t in 2011. The expected increase is the result of a capacity expansion through the completion of a 105,000t/y production line.  Total capacity now amounts to 210,000t/y, however, production remains below capacity due to ongoing testing at the new US$349M plant in Luoyang City, Central Henan province.  In 2010, Chinalco Luoyang Copper Co. Ltd.’s production was 140,000t of copper plate and strip. 

## **Mine Production** 





- On 19<sup>th</sup> June, Chile’s northern electricity grid experienced an outage in two thirds of its system for several hours.  The grid provides power to many of the largest mines in Chile. **Anglo American** ’s and **Xstrata** ’s 465,000t/y **Collahuasi** mine experienced a small drop in daily production, having been forced to switch to backup power supply that day. Production at **Barrick Gold** ’s **Zaldivar** mine and **Codelco** ’s **Radomiro Tomic** and **Chuqicamata** mines was also mildly affected. All mines have since returned to normal output. 

- The management of **Codelco** ’s **Chuquicamata** mine has been threatened with strike action by the workers’ union.  The threat comes in response to workers’ fears of extensive redundancies after the mine shifts from open pit to underground operations in 2018.  The union is demanding that Codelco organise a meeting between management and workers in order to clarify the company’s position on the future of the operation.   On 15<sup>th</sup> June, 1,000 workers held a demonstration and a 5-hour road block took place on 22<sup>nd</sup> June.  Production at the mine has not been affected yet.  In 2011,

- It has been announced that the **Copper Mountain** project, located in British Columbia, Canada, has been completed and that production commenced on 4<sup>th</sup> June 2011 following final equipment adjustments. ## **Smelting and Refining** 





- **Mitsubishi Materials Corp.** announced on 10<sup>th</sup> June 2011 that it is planning to resume operations at its **Onahama** smelting plant from 1<sup>st</sup> July 2011.  The plant has been shut down since the 11<sup>th</sup> March earthquake.  The company expects that the plant will return to full capacity by September.  In 2010, the plant produced 220,000t of blister copper and accounted for around 15% of Japan’s copper output. It has also been reported that overall, Japanese smelters plan a 21% y-o-y reduction in output in 2011, mainly as a result of the consequences of the 11th March earthquake. 

- Zambia’s largest copper miner, **Kansanshi Copper Mines** , which is owned by **First Quantum Minerals

** , has announced plans to build a copper smelting plant with a copper concentrate processing capacity of 1.2Mt/y. The plant will be located in the Northwestern Province and will be developed at a cost of US$500M.  A feasibility study is currently underway and a final decision on the project is expected to be made by the board of directors by October.  Through the move, the company hopes to cut costs and end over-reliance on smelters in the Copperbelt region.
